notes.introduction: We see an immense variety of objects around us. Every object is made up of one or more materials such as glass, metal, plastic, wood, cotton, paper, mud, or soil. Sorting materials into groups based on their similarities and differences helps us study their properties systematically.
keyPoints: Objects around us are made of a wide variety of materials.
A given material could be used to make many different objects (e.g., wood can be used for chairs, tables, doors, and bats).
An object could also be made of a single material or multiple materials.
Materials are grouped together on the basis of similarities and differences in their properties.
Properties of materials include Appearance (lustre), Hardness, Solubility, Float/Sink behavior, and Transparency.
Metals have a special shine called lustre (e.g., iron, copper, gold, aluminium), whereas non-metals often look dull.
Hard materials are difficult to compress or scratch (e.g., iron, stone), while soft materials can be easily compressed or scratched (e.g., sponge, cotton).
Substances that completely dissolve in water are soluble (e.g., salt, sugar), while those that do not dissolve are insoluble (e.g., sand, chalk powder).
Liquids can also be miscible (mix completely, like vinegar or lemon juice) or immiscible (do not mix, like mustard oil or kerosene).
Materials may float on water (e.g., dry leaf, wood) or sink in water (e.g., stone, iron nail).

Transparent materials allow light to pass through them completely (glass, clear water); opaque materials do not allow light to pass (wood, cardboard); translucent materials allow light to pass partially (oiled paper, frosted glass).
